title: The woman and the dragon (Revelation 12)
hook: a woman clothed with the sun, a dragon, and a child snatched up to safety

segments.voice: Yesterday, two witnesses lay in the street, then stood up, and heaven sang that the kingdoms of this world are his. Your line was he shall reign. Who did you tell about something good you'd seen? Day one thousand three hundred four.

"And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars." She's in labor, crying out. Then a second sign: a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, so huge its tail sweeps stars out of the sky. It plants itself in front of her and waits, ready to devour the baby the moment it's born. The child comes. And before the dragon can move, the child is caught up to God and to his throne. The woman runs into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared for her. Today's word is the two of them: the woman and the dragon.
screen: `THE CHILD IS CAUGHT UP TO GOD.`

segments.voice: First, who is she? Revelation doesn't put a name tag on her, and Christians read her in more than one way. Catholic tradition sees in her Mary, the mother of the child who rules, and also the church, and Orthodox writers have read her both ways too. Some Protestant readers see God's people: Israel, who brought the Messiah into the world, and the church that follows. Some hold all of these at once. The text leaves room for each. Second, the war. Next comes "war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon." And the dragon, the text says, "prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven." He's thrown down. Revelation even names him: that old serpent, the devil. Third, how he's beaten. Not by a bigger dragon. A voice in heaven says the faithful "overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony." A slain Lamb and people telling the truth. That's the weapon. Fourth, the earth helps. The dragon pours a flood out of its mouth to sweep the woman away, and "the earth helped the woman, and the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed up the flood." The ground itself takes her side. So for all its monsters, the chapter keeps its eye on a mother. She's in danger every time she appears. She runs, she hides, she's chased. And she's kept. The dragon is furious, but it doesn't get the child, and it doesn't get her.
screen: `BEATEN BY THE LAMB AND THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for mothers in danger, or hold them in mind if you don't pray. Settle, and breathe. Think of mothers running with their children right now: from war, from a violent home, from hunger, through a desert or across a sea. Think of one woman giving birth tonight with no one safe beside her. Then, if one comes to mind, someone you know who's carrying a child or carrying a family alone. Hold her by name. If you pray, you can ask that she be given a place prepared, like the woman in the wilderness. The bell holds the time.
The woman and the dragon. Revelation twelve's picture of a mother and her child under threat, a dragon thrown down, and a woman kept safe in the wilderness.
screen: `THE WOMAN AND THE DRAGON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the dragon loses. Today, be a bit of earth that helps: one thing, however small, for a mother who's carrying too much. Day one thousand three hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholic Christians hear Revelation 12 read on feasts of Mary, and Christian art has pictured her clothed with the sun and crowned with stars; some Protestant preachers read it as the story of God's people kept safe in trouble.

original.note: Greek: dragon, a great serpent. Revelation 12 calls him that old serpent, the devil.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fantasy battle with a monster.
what it means: a mother and child threatened by evil, and kept safe; the dragon is thrown down by the Lamb and the truth.
what a scholar hears: that old serpent: Revelation ties the dragon back to the serpent of Genesis, and the woman's child to the one who rules the nations.

notes: Readings of the woman: Catholic and Orthodox (Mary, and the church), Protestant (Israel and the church), some hold all. Confirm fair to each.
Seven heads, ten horns, tail sweeping stars (12:3–4) and 'that old serpent, the devil' (12:9) are paraphrased from the chapter.
howItsDone: Revelation 12 is read at Marian feasts (e.g., the Assumption in the Catholic lectionary); stated generally. Confirm wording for the Orthodox, and 'more often' for Protestants.
Practice mentions mothers fleeing war, violence and hunger; confirm tone is careful and not used for drama.
Editor pass: Mary reading reworded so Catholic tradition and Orthodox writers are not overstated; garbled 'which is why' line rewritten; stock phrase trimmed.
Audit 2026-10-02: 'in danger the whole chapter' overstated (she is absent from 12:7–12); now 'every time she appears'.
